title: Surgical Management of Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
summary: An exhaustive guide to the indications, techniques, and complications of retinal detachment surgery, covering Pneumatic Retinopexy, Scleral Buckling, and the critical factors for surgical success and failure.

sections.title: Indications for Urgent Surgery
content: Acutely symptomatic RD: Should be surgically repaired as soon as possible, particularly if the macula is not involved (Fig. 16.22A).
Superior or large break: Increases urgency as Subretinal Fluid (SRF) is likely to spread more rapidly.
Advanced syneresis: Found in high myopia, increasing the urgency of intervention.
Impossible visualization: Patients with dense fresh vitreous haemorrhage where fundus visualization is impossible require surgery ASAP if B-scan ultrasonography shows an underlying RD.
Macular Threat: Urgent surgery is needed in an acute progressive RD if the macula is threatened.
Macula-off timing: Visual results are better if surgery is performed within 72 hours, even if the macula is already off.

sections.title: Pre-Operative Preparation
content: Step 1: NPO Status - The patient should not eat or drink if urgent surgery is contemplated.
Step 2: Activity Modification - Minimizing activity may be helpful.
Step 3: Posturing - Bed-rest with the head turned so the retinal break is in the most dependent position.
Benefit: Reduces the amount of SRF and facilitates surgery.

rows: Outpatient procedure using intravitreal gas bubble + cryotherapy or laser to seal break without scleral buckling.
Success rates are worse than those achievable with conventional scleral buckling.
Uncomplicated RD, small retinal break, or cluster of breaks < 2 clock hours in the upper 2/3 of peripheral retina.

sections.title: Pneumatic Retinopexy: Visual Sequence
content: A: Cryotherapy is applied.
B: Gas injection into the vitreous cavity.
C: Gas seals the retinal break and the retina becomes flat.
D: Gas is eventually absorbed.
Observation: Gas bubble breakup can lead to 'fish eggs' appearance.

sections.title: Principles of Scleral Buckling
sections.content: Scleral buckling (conventional/external RD surgery) involves suturing material (explant) onto the sclera to create an inward indentation (buckle). The purpose is to close retinal breaks by opposing the RPE to the sensory retina and to reduce dynamic vitreoretinal traction at sites of local vitreoretinal adhesion. This technique should ALWAYS be used for patients with detachment secondary to post-traumatic dialysis.

sections.title: Scleral Buckling Explant & Configuration
content: Materials: Soft or hard silicone.
Sizing: Entire break should be surrounded by approx 2 mm of buckle.
Anterior Extension: Buckle must involve the area of the vitreous base anterior to the tear to prevent reopening/leakage.
Measurement: Break dimensions are assessed by comparing them with the optic disc diameter.
Configurations: Radial, segmental, circumferential, or encircling (depending on size/position/number of breaks).

sections.title: Buckling Surgical Technique
content: 1. Peritomy: Conjunctiva is incised to facilitate access.
2. Localization: Retinal breaks are localized (Fig 16.30A).
3. Cryotherapy: Applied to the localized break.
4. Explant Placement: Appropriate dimensions/orientation sutured to sclera (mattress sutures common).
5. Verification: Position of buckle checked in relation to the break.

rows: Drainage-Air-Cryotherapy-Explant; advocates cite rapid reattachment in deep or longstanding viscous SRF.
Retinal perforation, retinal incarceration in the drainage site, or choroidal haemorrhage.
Some practitioners prefer Pars Plana Vitrectomy as a primary option to avoid external drainage complications.

sections.title: Complications of Scleral Buckling
content: Diplopia: Due to mechanical effect; common; early spontaneous resolution typical, but intervention may be needed.
Cystoid Macular Oedema (CMO): Occurs in up to 25%; usually responds to treatment.
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM): Occurs in around 15%.
Foveal Complications: Persistent subfoveal fluid and structural disruption (usually in macula-off detachments).
Anterior Segment Ischaemia: Vascular compromise risk; higher with encircling bands and sickle haemoglobinopathies.
Buckle-Related: Extrusion, intrusion, or infection (requires removal and antibiotics).
Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Early spikes (usually resolve) or persistent elevation; potential angle closure.
Choroidal Detachment: Usually resolves spontaneously as oedema settles and vortex vein function improves.

branches: Missed Breaks (requires thorough search if RD configuration doesn't match primary break)
Buckle Failure (Inadequate size, incorrect positioning, or inadequate height)
Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR) - Most common late failure; traction opens old/new breaks; occurs weeks post-op
Fish-mouthing (Large superior equatorial U-tear in bullous RD opens widely post-buckling)
Reopening of Break (Inadequate cryo/buckling, or decrease in buckle height over time/removal)

sections.title: Managing Buckle Failure
content: Incorrect size/position: Requires replacement or repositioning of explant.
Inadequate height: May be addressed by SRF drainage, intravitreal gas injection, or Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) as a definitive measure.

sections.title: CRITICAL RECALL: The Three Commonest Causes of Failure

content.explanation: P: Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR). C: failure to Close all breaks. N: development of New breaks.
